coherence.reasons: Both run a consistent line from diagnosis (same margin bridge) through levers, a sized bridge, sequencing and board decisions. Y's hierarchy is slightly tighter: "not mainly wages" leads to six levers, one bridge to 2.96%, a head-to-head with the draft plan, then waves and decisions. X is also well structured, and its split between a data-backed base (2.5%) and the full plan (3.0%) is a useful logical layer. But X detours on slide 3 into a team-invented 'margin, not wages' kick-off hypothesis that is not in the pack, and its headline "rather than cutting labor" sits awkwardly with a 3% net hours reduction as its third lever. Y has one loose link: it equates the $10.4M incremental e-commerce loss with the 0.84-pt fulfillment drag. The difference is small.

judgment.reasons: Both land on the key's preferred recommendation (R1) with targeted labor action, promotion pruning with ValuMart guardrails, delivery repricing that honours the owners, and staged closures respecting the board vote. X weighs alternatives more fully: four options, including deeper promotions and exiting home delivery (sized at up to +$6M and held as a fallback because of the owner commitment), plus an explicit 'why not exit all nine now' argument. X also separates levers resting on Harlow's own data from those needing negotiation or a vote, gives a promotion break-even (41% volume loss), and quantifies each risk's effect on FY2028 margin, including a combined downside of 2.32%. Y compares only the draft plan against its own, though it has good trigger-based risk responses, a fix-or-exit rule and a pragmatic lender briefing and waiver request. Y's contingency list includes 'wage pass-through below the full bill', which is a hope rather than a lever, and its private-label pace is more aggressive. X's trade-off treatment is the more defensible.

evidence.reasons: Both reproduce the required calculations correctly: margin by year, the driver bridge with labor at 13%, the e-commerce drag of $10.4M, closure gain of $6.6M and a target of about $42M on post-closure sales. Both also dismantle the 6.1% claim and the category team's correlation the same way. X uses the critical evidence more deeply: it splits the labor change into wage (+1.11 pt) and productivity (−0.77 pt) effects, reconciles its e-commerce model to Table 1 in every year, computes break-even delivery fee and per-order losses after repricing, and gives a phased in-year FY2026 bridge with stated capture rates. X's weak points are the claim that deeper promotions 'did not protect' ValuMart stores (no counterfactual) and somewhat optimistic in-year capture. Y is more careful on that inference and flags that the comparison lacks store controls, but wrongly equates the ~8% incremental channel loss with the 0.84-pt fulfillment drag and assumes the chain reaches Q4 shrink while trimming hours. Both flag their vendor-pool and cost allowances as assumptions. X has a small net edge.

revision.reasons: Both correctly revise the CFO/COO view: wages rose 9.4% but labor explains only 0.30 of 2.35 points, the 8% cut risks shrink, and the freeze locks in the e-commerce loss. Both keep the supported part, replacing the blanket cut with targeted scheduling to absorb the 2027 wage step. X goes further: it quantifies the wage versus productivity effects, shows about $12M was already taken out through productivity (and links that to rising shrink), and runs management's plan through the same model against both the covenant ($19–24M) and the target (0.9–1.2%). X also tests and partly revises its own counter-hypothesis (commercial fixes alone reach only 1.8%). That framing mislabels the 'initial hypothesis' relative to the pack, which is a blemish, but the handling of management's view is the more rigorous. Y is direct and correct ("why labor looks like the cause", draft versus recommended table), with less depth.

overall.reasons: The two documents share the diagnosis and nearly the same lever set and sizing, so the gap is modest. X would serve the CEO somewhat better: it gives an explicit in-year FY2026 covenant bridge, shows how much of the 3.0% rests on proven versus negotiated levers, sizes the option of exiting delivery, quantifies sensitivities and the combined downside, and tests management's plan on the same model. Y is tighter and adds real practical value with the lender briefing, trigger-based risk register and a fix-or-exit rule the board can vote on immediately. Its reading that FY2026 has already closed is defensible given the pack's ambiguous calendar, but it leaves the covenant answered only on a run-rate basis. Both acknowledge the plan is thin at 3.0%. X's deeper weighing of alternatives and risks outweighs Y's cleaner structure.
